content: CD278, also known as Inducible T-cell Costimulator (ICOS), is an immune checkpoint protein encoded by the ICOS gene in humans. It is a member of the CD28 superfamily of costimulatory molecules and is expressed on activated T cells. ICOS is particularly important for the function of T-helper 2 (Th2) cells. The protein encoded by the ICOS gene belongs to the CD28 and CTLA-4 family of cell-surface receptors. It forms homodimers and plays a critical role in cell-to-cell signaling, immune responses, and the regulation of cell proliferation. In knockout studies, ICOS-deficient (ICOS-/-) T cells, when activated with plate-bound anti-CD3, exhibit reduced proliferation and decreased secretion of interleukin-2 (IL-2). This defect in proliferation can be rescued by adding IL-2 to the culture, suggesting that the proliferative impairment is due to either ICOS-mediated IL-2 secretion or the activation of similar signaling pathways between ICOS and IL-2. Regarding cytokine secretion, ICOS-/CD4+ T cells activated in vitro show reduced secretion of IL-4, a Th2-associated cytokine, while maintaining normal levels of interferon-gamma (IFN-γ), a Th1-associated cytokine. Similarly, CD4+ T cells isolated from ICOS-/mice immunized with keyhole limpet hemocyanin (KLH) in alum or complete Freund's adjuvant exhibit diminished IL-4 secretion upon recall with KLH, but their IFN-γ and IL-5 secretion remain comparable to wild-type cells. These findings are consistent with observations in an airway hypersensitivity model, where ICOS-/mice show reduced IL-4 secretion but normal IL-5 secretion in response to sensitization with ovalbumin (Ova) protein. This indicates a specific defect in Th2 cytokine secretion, without impairing Th1 differentiation, as both IL-4 and IL-5 are Th2-associated cytokines. In line with the reduced Th2 responses, ICOS-/mice demonstrate impaired germinal center formation and reduced levels of IgG1 and IgE antibodies following immunization. In the context of combination therapy, patients treated with ipilimumab (an anti-CTLA-4 antibody) exhibit increased levels of ICOS+ T cells in both tumor tissues and blood. This increase serves as a pharmacodynamic biomarker of anti-CTLA-4 treatment. In wild-type C57BL/6 mice, anti-CTLA-4 therapy results in tumor rejection in 80–90% of cases. However, in gene-targeted mice deficient in either ICOS or its ligand (ICOSLG), the efficacy of anti-CTLA-4 therapy drops to less than 50%. Introducing an agonistic stimulus for the ICOS pathway during anti-CTLA-4 therapy significantly enhances treatment efficacy, increasing it by fourto fivefold compared to control treatments. As of 2015, antibodies targeting ICOS were not yet available for clinical testing.
